scope_notes: The eight cru pages are the evidence that eight separate delimitations exist. They are not evidence of a ninth, collective one.
statement: Northern Rhône is a collective name for the eight cru appellations of the Rhône corridor between Vienne and Valence — Côte-Rôtie, Condrieu, Château-Grillet, Saint-Joseph, Crozes-Hermitage, Hermitage, Cornas and Saint-Péray. Each of those eight is separately delimited by its own specification; no appellation, mention or delimited area named Northern Rhône exists, so CARTA holds the region as an editorial grouping with no legal boundary of its own.

Six of the eight crus sit on the Rhône's right, western bank — Côte-Rôtie, Condrieu, Château-Grillet, Saint-Joseph, Cornas and Saint-Péray — while Hermitage and Crozes-Hermitage sit on the left bank around Tain-l'Hermitage. Bank is an orientation fact and nothing more: it does not predict landform, substrate or permitted grape.

The eight crus were recognised across two decades and never as one act: Château-Grillet and Saint-Péray by decrees of 8 December 1936, Crozes-Hermitage and Hermitage on 4 March 1937 (Hermitage having first been recognised as an appellation d'origine by a judgment of the tribunal de Valence on 25 June 1936), Cornas on 5 August 1938, Condrieu on 27 April 1940, Côte-Rôtie on 18 October 1940 and Saint-Joseph only on 15 June 1956. Different dates froze different rules.

Four grapes carry the whole corridor: Syrah is the only red variety permitted in any of the five red crus, Viognier is the sole variety of Condrieu and Château-Grillet and the only white admitted into a Côte-Rôtie red, and Marsanne and Roussanne are the white pair of Saint-Joseph, Crozes-Hermitage, Hermitage and Saint-Péray. The same four varieties are re-weighted by each specification rather than by geography.

quantity.scope: Cru appellations of the Rhône corridor between Vienne and Valence governed by CARTA

statement: CARTA governs eight cru appellations in the corridor.

The regional Côtes du Rhône AOP extends along the valley from the Vienne sector towards Avignon and overlaps the northern corridor. It is the legal home of fruit that the crus do not cover, which is why a vineyard can sit among the crus and still be sold under a broader name.

The active outlines in this world are INAO cartographic representations of eight regulatory geographical areas. They are not vineyard land, not parcel eligibility and not a Northern Rhône polygon; the region label is a derived orientation anchor over the mapped crus.

source_refs.locator: roughly 60 km north to south along the right bank

statement: The Rhône is the corridor's organising spine: the crus are strung along roughly sixty kilometres of its banks between Vienne and Valence, and it is the river's course that decides which slopes face the sun. It decides nothing about legal origin.

scope_notes: The hill's shape is physical evidence. It does not establish parcel eligibility for either appellation.
statement: INAO describes the Hermitage vineyard as sitting on a fragment of granitic massif separated from the Ardèche mountains by the Rhône, with south-facing hillsides terraced behind stone walls. The hill is one landform; Hermitage AOC and Crozes-Hermitage AOC are two legal areas that meet it differently.

scope_notes: Geological description only. No flavour, drainage or ripening consequence is asserted.
statement: The Saint-Péray specification describes a primary-era granitic basement over which secondary deposits built a limestone massif, leaving the Crussol relief standing above the appellation, with soils that mix calcareous, clay-limestone and granitic material.

scope_notes: Terrace age and sediment origin as stated by the specification. Nothing about wine style follows from it.
statement: The Crozes-Hermitage specification describes Les Chassis as the lowest and youngest of the Quaternary terraces, forming a triangle whose apex is at Pont-de-l'Isère and whose gravels were carried down by alpine rivers.

Côte-Rôtie was recognised as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 18 October 1940; the specification in force is the one homologated by the arrêté of 4 July 2024, published in the Journal officiel on 7 July 2024.
Côte-Rôtie may only be a still red wine.

scope_notes: A permission is not a practice. Many Côte-Rôtie wines contain no Viognier at all, and the rule says nothing about what any producer did in a given vintage.
statement: Syrah is the principal variety and must be at least 80% of the holding's encépagement; Viognier is the accessory variety, permitted in mixed plantings within the Syrah parcels up to 20% of the vines. Where both varieties are used the specification requires that the wine be "vinifiés par assemblage des raisins concernés" — assembled at the grape stage in the same proportion, not blended as finished wines.

The geographic area covers Ampuis, Saint-Cyr-sur-le-Rhône and Tupin-et-Semons in the Rhône department, on the right bank south of Vienne, where INAO records slopes steepening to 60% and terraces held by stone walls locally called cheys.
Condrieu was recognised as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 27 April 1940; the specification in force is the one homologated by the arrêté of 4 July 2024.
Condrieu is a still white wine and its specification states plainly that "les vins sont issus du cépage viognier B" — Viognier and nothing else.

The specification's own account describes a wine that was doux in the mid-nineteenth century and is in most cases sec, sometimes demi-sec, in its modern form, with confidential quantities of moelleux or doux made from overripe grapes when conditions allow. "Dry white Viognier" is therefore the usual case, not the legal definition.

The geographic area runs across seven communes and three departments: Condrieu in the Rhône; Chavanay, Malleval, Saint-Michel-sur-Rhône, Saint-Pierre-de-Bœuf and Vérin in the Loire; and Limony in the Ardèche. INAO gives the vineyard as roughly 100 hectares of terraced right-bank hillside.

scope_notes: Widely repeated trade accounts give the low point as about seven hectares around 1960. CARTA keeps the specification's figure and date and records the divergence rather than averaging them.
statement: The specification records phylloxera devastating the vineyard in 1893, then the First World War and industrial employment draining the labour the terraces needed, until by 1965 only some eight hectares remained. It records the vineyard climbing back past 140 hectares by 2010 after a long replanting and terrace-rebuilding effort.

Château-Grillet was recognised as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 8 December 1936, making it one of the corridor's two oldest cru recognitions; the specification in force is the one homologated by the arrêté of 4 July 2024.
Château-Grillet is a still white wine made from Viognier alone, over roughly 3.5 hectares in the communes of Saint-Michel-sur-Rhône and Vérin in the Loire department.

resolution_needed: Compare the two delimited areas against the INAO parcel delimitation before describing the physical relationship more precisely.
statement: The Château-Grillet specification says the vineyard "a la particularité d'être inséré au cœur même de celui de l'appellation d'origine contrôlée « Condrieu »" — inserted into the heart of the Condrieu vineyard. The INAO product surface instead places it just south of Condrieu. Physical description and delimited geography are not the same statement, and neither makes Château-Grillet a part of Condrieu: they are independently delimited appellations.

scope_notes: Substrate description only; no flavour or quality consequence is asserted.
statement: The specification describes sandy soils derived from primary-era granite, locally enriched with fine material beneath the château, over a fractured subsoil.

Artémis Domaines records that the Pinault family acquired Château Grillet in 2011 and describes it as one of the very few French monopole AOCs and one of the smallest. The specification's own historical account describes continuous ownership by a single family line from 1830, which is a statement about the estate's past, not about its ownership today.

Saint-Joseph was recognised as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 15 June 1956, the last of the eight crus to be created; the specification in force is the one homologated by the arrêté of 4 July 2024.

Saint-Joseph may be red or white. For reds the specification requires Syrah to be at least 90% of the holding's encépagement, with Marsanne and Roussanne permitted only as accessory varieties in mixed plantings within the Syrah parcels up to 10% of the vines, and wines made from both colours must be "vinifiés par assemblage des raisins concernés". Whites come from Marsanne and Roussanne.

quantity.scope: Communes in the Saint-Joseph geographic area recorded by the specification

statement: The geographic area covers 26 communes — 23 in the Ardèche and three in the Loire — strung over roughly sixty kilometres of right bank. One appellation name therefore covers a long sequence of different slopes rather than a single côte.

The specification records Saint-Joseph beginning in 1956 on six communes around Tournon, expanding in 1969 by twenty further communes reaching north to the Condrieu area, and then being significantly narrowed by parcel revisions approved on 9–10 February 1994 and 20 June 2018, which cut the delimited parcel area from about 6,800 to about 3,400 hectares. Today's outline is a made thing, not a timeless one.
Crozes-Hermitage was recognised as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 4 March 1937; the specification in force is the one homologated by the arrêté of 10 December 2024.

Crozes-Hermitage may be red or white. Reds require Syrah to be at least 85% of the encépagement, with Marsanne and Roussanne admitted as accessory varieties in mixed plantings up to 15% of the vines; whites are Marsanne and Roussanne.

The geographic area covers eleven Drôme communes on the left bank facing Tournon — Beaumont-Monteux, Chanos-Curson, Crozes-Hermitage, Erôme, Gervans, Larnage, Pont-de-l'Isère, La Roche-de-Glun, Serves-sur-Rhône, Tain-l'Hermitage and part of Mercurol-Veaunes. It is the largest of the eight crus and the least uniform.

scope_notes: Substrate description only. CARTA draws no line from rock type to flavour, quality or ripening.
statement: The specification splits the appellation in two. In the north the Rhône has cut down to the granite de Tournon between Crozes-Hermitage and Serves-sur-Rhône, and sandy clays and granitic arenas are held on the slopes by dry-stone terraces. In the south and east lie Quaternary terraces of alpine gravels, with loess locally at the Gervans quartier of Les Blancs and distinctive kaolin sands at Larnage.

resolution_needed: Date the parcel reselection from the homologating text rather than the specification's narrative prose.
scope_notes: The specification's own narrative is internally inconsistent about when the reselection concluded: it places the ten-year effort "dans les années 1990" while dating the endorsement to June 1989. CARTA records both and resolves neither.
statement: The 1937 decree limited the area to part of the single commune of Crozes-Hermitage; postwar prosperity and vineyard expansion took it to eleven communes by 1952. A later reselection of the parcels from which grapes may come cut the production potential from 4,800 to 3,200 hectares.

The Crozes-Hermitage specification identifies its northern granite as the same formation that appears across the Rhône around Tournon, in Saint-Joseph. Geology crosses the river and the appellation boundary; the law does not.

Hermitage was first recognised as an appellation d'origine by a judgment of the tribunal de Valence dated 25 June 1936 and then as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 4 March 1937; the specification in force is the one homologated by the arrêté of 10 December 2024.

atlas_presentation.label: Red, white and a third form

statement: Hermitage may be red or white, and white wines may additionally carry the vin de paille mention. Reds require Syrah to be at least 85% of the encépagement with Marsanne and Roussanne as accessory varieties; whites and vin de paille come from Marsanne and Roussanne.

The appellation covers three Drôme communes — Tain-l'Hermitage, Crozes-Hermitage and Larnage — on the left bank. The commune named Crozes-Hermitage therefore contains land in both appellations, which is exactly why a commune name cannot tell a reader which wine a parcel may make.

The vin de paille mention requires the grapes to be dried for at least 45 days between harvest and pressing, a minimum natural richness of 170 grams of sugar per litre — about 19.5% potential alcohol — and a yield of 15 hectolitres per hectare.
Cornas was recognised as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 5 August 1938; the specification in force is the one homologated by the arrêté of 4 July 2024.
The Cornas specification states that "les vins sont issus du cépage syrah N". Cornas is red only and admits no accessory or white variety at all — the single-variety outlier among the eight crus.

scope_notes: Substrate and shelter as described by the specification. Nothing about wine style follows from either.
statement: The specification describes most of the vineyard as sitting on soils weathered from primary eruptive rock of the granite family — the porphyritic granites of Tournon — in an amphitheatre open to the south and sheltered from the north by the Arlettes massif, terraced behind stone walls.

resolution_needed: A dated primary or archival record naming the 1952 cellar would resolve the three accounts.
statement: The Cornas specification records that the first bottling on behalf of a private cellar happened only in 1952, fourteen years after the appellation was recognised. Trade accounts variously credit Joseph Michel with pioneering domaine-bottled Cornas in 1956 and Auguste Clape with being the village's first producer to bottle his own wine in 1957. CARTA keeps the regulatory date and both attributions rather than choosing a founder.
Saint-Péray was recognised as an appellation d'origine contrôlée by the decree of 8 December 1936.

Saint-Péray is a white-wine appellation covering both "vins blancs tranquilles" and "vins blancs mousseux", the sparkling wines made by a second fermentation in bottle, from Marsanne and Roussanne, over the communes of Saint-Péray and Toulaud in the Ardèche. INAO gives sparkling wine as roughly a tenth of the volume.

scope_notes: Trade accounts commonly date the first sparkling Saint-Péray to 1829. CARTA carries the specification's 1828 trials and does not merge the two dates.
statement: The Saint-Péray specification traces bottle-fermentation experiments to a merchant's cellarmaster in 1730 and records Louis-Alexandre Faure conducting systematic trials on a hundred barrels in 1828, an innovation it describes as unique in the Rhône valley at the time.

resolution_needed: Confirm homologation and Journal officiel publication before treating the 2025 proposal as current law.
statement: A modification of the Saint-Péray specification was adopted by the Comité national des appellations d'origine relatives aux vins et aux boissons alcoolisées on 6 February 2025 and placed in the national opposition procedure. A proposal in opposition is not law: CARTA records it as a dated observation and does not present it as the rule in force.

scope_notes: Granite continues physically from Cornas into Saint-Péray while the permitted colour and grapes change completely. The rock does not explain the rule.
statement: The specification describes a primary granitic basement of the Massif Central, secondary limestone deposits that left the Crussol massif standing, and soils that combine calcareous, clay-limestone and granitic material where the Rhône later carved a collapse basin.

scope_notes: CARTA governs the category. Its mapped area remains external INAO context in this release; no CARTA geometry is asserted for it.
statement: Collines Rhodaniennes is an IGP of the Rhône corridor recorded in the INAO geographical-area dataset for still and primeur wine. It is the legal category under which several of the corridor's most discussed wines are sold, including the replanted Seyssuel vineyard, because no cru appellation covers them.

Viognier is the sole variety of Condrieu and of Château-Grillet, where both specifications say simply that the wines come from Viognier B. It is also the only white variety a Côte-Rôtie red may contain, and it appears in none of the other five crus' rules.

The Condrieu specification's account of the twentieth century — phylloxera in 1893, war, and industrial work drawing labour off the terraces — brought the variety's home appellation down to some eight hectares by 1965. Viognier's later international spread begins from that near-disappearance, not from abundance.

Marsanne is the corridor's principal white variety, named with Roussanne in the white rules of Saint-Joseph, Crozes-Hermitage, Hermitage and Saint-Péray, permitted as an accessory variety in the reds of the first three, and the basis of both the Hermitage vin de paille mention and traditional-method Saint-Péray.

scope_notes: A planting share inside one appellation. It is not a rule and not a regional figure.
statement: The Saint-Joseph specification notes that Marsanne accounts for about 95% of the appellation's white plantings — the two named white varieties are legally paired but not equally planted.

Roussanne is named alongside Marsanne in every white rule of the corridor — Saint-Joseph, Crozes-Hermitage, Hermitage, the Hermitage vin de paille mention and Saint-Péray — and as an accessory variety in three of the reds. Legal parity with Marsanne is not the same as equal planting.

Syrah is the only red variety permitted in any northern cru, but its legal weight changes at every boundary: sole variety in Cornas, at least 90% of the encépagement in Saint-Joseph, at least 85% in Crozes-Hermitage and Hermitage, and at least 80% in Côte-Rôtie, where a white variety may join it.

Four Northern Rhône specifications — Côte-Rôtie, Saint-Joseph, Crozes-Hermitage and Hermitage — require that wines made from both the red and the white permitted varieties be "vinifiés par assemblage des raisins concernés": assembled as grapes, in the same proportion, rather than blended after fermentation. The rule governs when the varieties may meet, not whether any given producer uses the white grape at all.

Saint-Péray's sparkling wines are made by a second fermentation in the bottle. Domaine Alain Voge's Les Bulles d'Alain is a documented current example: 100% Marsanne, brut nature, with four years on lattes.

The Saint-Péray specification records Louis-Alexandre Faure carrying out systematic bottle-fermentation trials on a hundred barrels in 1828, following an earlier experiment by a merchant's cellarmaster in 1730, and treats this as the beginning of the reputation that sparkling Saint-Péray carried through the nineteenth century.

scope_notes: No ownership, purchase or inheritance is asserted for the Chaillot parcel or for Michel's cave.
statement: Rosenthal Wine Merchant records that when Robert Michel retired after the 2006 vintage he "leased his prime parcel in the Chaillot vineyard" to Guillaume Gilles and "provided his cave" for Gilles's use. A lease is a tenure arrangement, not a sale: CARTA records farming and use, and asserts no transfer of ownership of either the parcel or the cellar.

scope_notes: Traditional and low-intervention practice is not evidence of natural-wine membership, and the source language is not self-description.
statement: Rosenthal describes Gilles eschewing the destemmer in virtually all cases, working the vineyards by hand, using the grapes' own yeasts, ageing in old demi-muids and bottling without fining or filtration. These are concrete practices attributed to a producer, not a movement identity.

The Rare Wine Co. records the Michel family growing in Cornas for more than four hundred years, Robert's father Joseph as a pioneer of domaine-bottled Cornas in 1956, Robert taking over the family holding in 1975 at twenty-nine, and the vineyard growing from the 1.5 hectares his father farmed to about eight by the time he retired after the 2006 vintage.

Michel's wines came from Chaillot, Reynard and Tézier for the Cuvée des Coteaux and from La Geynale, described as a prized sub-cru high on the Reynard slope planted by his grandfather in 1910. He fermented long and whole-cluster for La Geynale and destemmed part of the Chaillot fruit, ageing in neutral demi-muids and pièces.

The Rare Wine Co. records Noël Verset working Chaillots, Sabarotte and Champelrose, beginning to divest his vines in the late 1980s, selling his largest parcel in 2001 as he neared ninety, and making wine under his own name until 2006. Reynard vines went to Thierry Allemand, Sabarotte to Clape and Courbis, and a half hectare in Chaillots planted in 1912 to his nephew Franck Balthazar.
Verset's method is recorded as fully ripe low-yield fruit, no destemming, crushing by foot, fifteen to eighteen days in small concrete vats and basket pressing.

The Rare Wine Co. records that Thierry Allemand worked during the day for Joseph Michel and then for Michel's son Robert, while working nights helping Noël Verset, and that Verset later sold him some of his Reynard vines dating to the beginning of the twentieth century.

scope_notes: CARTA records WORKED_FOR and WORKED_WITH here and declines to promote either into MENTORED_BY.
statement: The same importer that documents Allemand's work with the elder Cornas growers states plainly that he "is a disciple of no one's" and describes his approach as uniquely his while deeply rooted in the past. Working for someone is not being mentored by them.

scope_notes: An episodic unsulfured cuvée is not an estate-wide identity, and CARTA does not classify Allemand as a natural-wine producer on this evidence.
statement: Allemand is described as using as little sulfur as possible, ageing eighteen months to two years on lees without racking, and having released a Sans Soufre bottling in only five vintages seen by his importer: 1998, 1999, 2001, 2004 and 2011. Low sulfur here is a practice inside a source-described traditional framework, not a movement label.

scope_notes: Kinship plus shared vinification is not mentorship. CARTA records FAMILY_OF and WORKED_WITH and does not add MENTORED_BY.
statement: Polaner Selections records that Vincent Paris's uncle is Robert Michel, that his first vintage was 1997, that he made his first two wines with his uncle before renting facilities of his own, that he inherited most of his vines from his grandfather, and that he rented and then purchased vines from his uncle including Geynale in the Cornas amphitheatre.

resolution_needed: Reconcile the Verset-to-Balthazar Chaillot parcel against parcel-level records before asserting a single planting date or a single parcel identity.
scope_notes: The two accounts of the Chaillot parcel differ on planting date — 1912 in the Verset article, 1914 in the Balthazar profile — and CARTA does not reconcile them without parcel-level evidence.
statement: The Rare Wine Co. records Franck Balthazar leaving a textile factory in 2002 to take up Cornas, acquiring a planting of Petite Syrah in the Chaillot vineyard from Noël Verset alongside half-century-old family vines in Mazards and La Côte, ploughing with a horse, and fermenting whole-cluster with native yeasts in concrete before neutral demi-muids.

scope_notes: The Cornas specification dates the first bottling for a private cellar to 1952 and another importer credits Joseph Michel in 1956. CARTA carries all three.
statement: The Rare Wine Co. records Auguste Clape as the village's first producer to bottle his own wine in 1957, having previously sold in barrel to négociants, with his son Pierre-Marie working alongside him from 1989 and grandson Olivier following. The domaine acquired century-old vines from Noël Verset.

Old-vine fruit is not destemmed, primary fermentation runs six to seven days in concrete, ageing uses old neutral demi-muids and pièces with no new oak, and the flagship Cornas is blended from five or six cuvées of the oldest vines. A Côtes du Rhône bottling includes fruit from 120-year-old vines near Saint-Péray together with declassified Cornas.

scope_notes: Emma Amsellem's arrival in the estate's current generation was reported in the research handoff but is not carried by the sources accepted here; CARTA leaves it out rather than dating it loosely.
statement: The estate's own chronology has Francis Vernay creating the domaine at Condrieu and planting its first vines at the Coteau de Vernon, releasing a first Coteau de Vernon cuvée in 1940; Georges Vernay taking over from his father in 1953; and Christine Vernay taking over in 1996, adding Terrasses de l'Empire and the estate's first red cuvées.

scope_notes: CARTA carries a documented leading role. "Georges Vernay saved Viognier" is attributed cultural shorthand from the estate and the trade, not a sole-causal finding: the same recovery involved Francis Vernay's earlier planting, André Perret's 1980s development work, Yves Cuilleron's generation and a wider replanting effort.
statement: The Syndicat des Vignerons de l'AOC Condrieu describes Georges Vernay as a man of vision and conviction who "worked hard to rebuild the hillsides and rescue the Viognier grape variety from obscurity", earning the nickname of the Pope of Condrieu. His own estate says he is globally recognised as having saved the abandoned variety and that he replanted his land and revitalised a generation of growers.

The Condrieu growers' organisation records Christine Vernay finishing the reconstruction of the Coteau de Vernon and converting the whole domaine to organic growing, across a range that spans the Côte-Rôtie, Condrieu and Saint-Joseph appellations, with the oldest vines dating to the hectare of Viognier Francis Vernay planted on the Coteau de Vernon in the 1930s.

The Condrieu growers' organisation records André Perret returning to the area to plant vines and develop the Condrieu AOC in the 1980s, with a first estate vintage in 1983, and a domaine of thirteen hectares of which 5.5 are in Condrieu, including the Coteau de Chéry and Clos Chanson bottlings.

The Condrieu growers' organisation records Yves Cuilleron taking over the family domaine in 1987 when it held 3.5 hectares in Condrieu and Saint-Joseph, and the estate reaching ninety hectares across six Northern Rhône AOCs plus IGP and Vin de France wines.

The Condrieu growers' organisation records that Yves Cuilleron, Pierre Gaillard and François Villard began the project in 1996 to revive the old Seyssuel vineyard north of Vienne, producing a first vintage in 1998, and that the project farms twelve hectares of Seyssuel hillside planted to Syrah and Viognier.

scope_notes: Cultural adjacency to Côte-Rôtie is not legal equivalence, and Seyssuel is not a ninth cru.
statement: Sotanum, with Héluicum and Taburnum, is sold as an IGP Collines Rhodaniennes wine. Seyssuel's slopes sit in the same corridor as the crus and are farmed by three cru producers, and the wine is still not a cru wine, because no cru appellation covers that ground.

René-Jean Dard's own account gives 1983 as the first vintage he and François Ribo made together, and 1984 as the year they "began properly". CARTA keeps both: they are two different events, not one contested date.

Dard describes the estate being assembled by renting vineyards from their owners and expanding gradually across parcels in Crozes-Hermitage, Hermitage and Saint-Joseph. A single cellar point cannot stand in for that patchwork, and rented land is not owned land.

Dard describes deciding to plough rather than use herbicides from the mid-1980s, and says explicitly that what interests them is "the notion of working cleanly" rather than holding an organic certification or a logo for the label. Absence of certification here is a stated choice, not evidence of conventional farming.

scope_notes: A tendency with a stated exception, not a fixed recipe applied to every wine and vintage.
statement: Reds are described as ten to fifteen days of maceration with whole bunches — unless sunburn requires sorting, in which case a destemmer is used — fermented in large wood with the cap broken once a day and aged in 500-litre demi-muids; whites are pressed whole-bunch.

scope_notes: This is the producer's own position. CARTA records a deep low-sulfur history alongside an explicit refusal of zero-sulfur absolutism, and does not encode either as a category.
statement: Dard told Louis/Dressner that making natural wine "should not be a goal unto itself" but "a tool to make qualitatively superior wine", and that he had made sulfur-free wines since he was fifteen, following his father. He told LITTLEWINE that their goal is not to make wine without sulfites but to make good wine, and that if a wine is going a bit wild they do not stop themselves adding some.

scope_notes: Precursor of barrel vinification and élevage in Saint-Péray. Not the invention of still Saint-Péray, which the same passage says already existed in tank.
statement: The estate records the Ongrie cuvée as created in 1984, 100% Marsanne, vinified exclusively in 228- and 400-litre oak, at a time when "l'essentiel de la production de Saint-Péray était issue de la méthode traditionnelle et les vins étaient vinifiés en cuves" — most Saint-Péray was sparkling and still wines were made in tank. The estate describes Alain Voge as the precursor of barrel work in Saint-Péray.

Les Bulles d'Alain is 100% Marsanne, méthode traditionnelle, brut nature, with a second fermentation in bottle and four years on lattes. The estate says it perpetuates the traditional-method Saint-Péray that made the region's reputation from the 1830s.

One estate holds both of Saint-Péray's wine forms at once: a traditional-method sparkling wine presented as the continuation of the appellation's nineteenth-century reputation, and a barrel-vinified still wine created in 1984 as a deliberate departure from what most of the appellation was then doing. The domaine also works Cornas.

The Rare Wine Co. places Gonon, with Gripa and Chave, among the last old-school Saint-Joseph growers based in the original appellation around Tournon, Mauves and Saint-Jean-de-Muzols, records the brothers buying Raymond Trollat's 1915 planting on his retirement, and describes Marsanne planted by their father at the Coteau des Oliviers in 1958 and Roussanne in 1974.

The brothers are described as working organically, ploughing the steep slopes by horse, replanting by sélection massale from their own old vines, fermenting reds up to three weeks whole-cluster in open wooden vats and ageing in old 600-litre foudres.

scope_notes: A reference-guide entry rather than a first-party or specialist source; the family chronology is carried at that fitness.
statement: The Guide Hachette records the Gripa family arriving at Saint-Péray in the seventeenth century and settling at Mauves around 1850, Fabrice Gripa running the domaine since 2001 after his father Bernard, and eighteen hectares spanning Saint-Joseph and Saint-Péray with the Les Figuiers, Les Pins and Le Berceau cuvées.

scope_notes: This is the corridor's clearest producer-base-versus-vineyard-geography case. Arlebosc is not in Saint-Joseph in any legal sense.
statement: Hervé Souhaut created Domaine Romaneaux-Destezet with Béatrice Souhaut in 1993, based at Arlebosc in the Ardèche hills above Saint-Joseph. The estate's range includes Saint-Joseph Syrah alongside Vallée du Doux wines: the producer's base sits outside the Saint-Joseph geography, and the base point must never be read as the location of the Saint-Joseph vines.

scope_notes: No natural-wine self-identification was captured; CARTA records concrete practice and the association, not membership.
statement: Souhaut's importer describes whole-bunch fermentation with no destemming, spontaneous fermentation without added yeast, gentle hand punch-downs rather than heavy pumping over, and sulfur limited to about 25 mg/L. This is an importer's description of practice, not the producer's own account of an identity.

Skurnik records Alain Graillot returning home to Crozes-Hermitage to start his own domaine in 1985, and his sons Maxime and Antoine being in charge since 2008, with hand harvesting, organic farming, whole-cluster fermentation and ageing in one- to three-year-old barrels bought from Burgundy estates.

scope_notes: Northern Crozes-Hermitage is hill and granite country. The appellation's southern terraces are a different landscape under the same name.
statement: Skurnik records a sixth-generation family estate at Gervans, Laurent Fayolle taking control in 2002 when his father and uncle divided the family domaine among their children, and seven hectares of parcels — many over sixty years old — in the granite hills behind the hill of Hermitage, across Crozes-Hermitage, Hermitage and Saint-Péray.

scope_notes: A blending philosophy across sites, not a claim that any one site is better than another.
statement: The Rare Wine Co. records Chave making Hermitage since 1481, the current generation being father Gérard and son Jean-Louis, and the flagship red being assembled from the domaine's several Hermitage sites — "Bessards is our essential climat; you can't make a Grand Hermitage without it" — with the blend rebuilt from zero each year. The domaine also makes a Saint-Joseph rouge from vines in the historic centre of that appellation.

scope_notes: Named-parcel bottling and a multi-site blend are two ways of organising the same hill. Neither is presented here as better.
statement: The house dates itself to the 1808 creation of Calvet et Compagnie in the rue de l'Hermitage at Tain, records Michel Chapoutier creating the first plot selections — Sélections Parcellaires — in 1989, and his taking control in 1990 and beginning to apply biodynamic cultivation.

The house records its founding in 1834 by Antoine Jaboulet on the hill of l'Hermitage at Tain, the creation of Hermitage La Chapelle in 1961, Gérard Jaboulet taking up the torch from 1977 until his death in 1997, and Caroline Frey assuming control in 2006 and beginning the conversion to organic and biodynamic farming. A historic house identity survived a change of owning family.

Maison Guigal records its founding by Etienne Guigal at Ampuis in 1946, Marcel Guigal taking over management in 1961 when his father lost his sight, Philippe Guigal joining as winemaker in 1997, a run of acquisitions including Vidal-Fleury, Château d'Ampuis, Jean-Louis Grippat, de Vallouit and Domaine de Bonserine, and its own cooperage from 2003. Scale, négoce and acquisition are part of this corridor's real ecology.

scope_notes: A parcel mosaic assembled into one wine, at the opposite end of the scale from a single half-hectare on the Côte Brune.
statement: The Rare Wine Co. records the Jamet brothers taking charge of the family domaine when their father Joseph retired in the mid-1980s, farming twenty-five plots across seventeen lieux-dits, and choosing each year which of those sites enter the flagship wine, with mostly whole-cluster fermentation and about 20% new wood.

iDealwine records that Jean-Michel Stéphan established his domaine at Tupin-Semons in Côte-Rôtie in 1991 after working at Domaine des Terres Dorées, Jean-Paul Brun's estate in Beaujolais — a documented professional route between two CARTA worlds.

scope_notes: External attribution of a natural-wine identity is recorded as attribution. The later meeting with Yvon Métras and Marcel Lapierre reported by the same source is chronology, not evidence of a transmission relationship, and CARTA adds none.
statement: The same source records that Stéphan has added no sulfites since 1997, ferments with indigenous yeasts using carbonic maceration, ages in old barrels and neither fines nor filters, with his largest plot on the granite and gneiss terraces of Bassenon and replanting by massale selection of Sérine. Trade sources describe this work as natural; no self-description was captured.

The estate records Stéphane Robert creating Domaine du Tunnel in 1994 with 2.5 hectares, working Cornas, Saint-Péray and Saint-Joseph and adding Condrieu in 2013, reaching about twelve hectares, and taking its name from a 170-metre early-twentieth-century railway tunnel it rehabilitated at the lieu-dit Barras in Saint-Péray.
